```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6,
  fig.height = 4, dpi = 100)
library(spax)
library(ggplot2)
```

Choose a model by the quantity you need and the observations that can support
it. spax retains its public floating catchment area (FCA) workflow and adds an
experimental corrected static conditional-logit allocation workflow with an
explicit outside option. Existing FCA calls remain valid; they do not need to
be rewritten as allocation fits.

| Question | Starting point | What the output means |
|:--|:--|:--|
| How is weighted supply distributed relative to weighted demand? | `spax_2sfca()`, `spax_e2sfca()`, `spax_m2sfca()` | A model-specific supply-per-demand accessibility index |
| How are request opportunities allocated among facilities and an outside option? | `prepare_allocation()` then `clm_allocation()` | Choice probabilities and expected loads under a declared model |
| Which parameters fit observed utilization or flows? | `fit_allocation()` with an explicit loss and starts | A calibrated mean model plus optimization diagnostics |
| What changes under a supply scenario at the same parameters? | Reprepare and `evaluate_allocation()` | A model-based contrast, not an estimated causal effect |
| What can be predicted at additional locations? | `predict_allocation()` | Requested outputs with probability, demand and capacity validity flags |
| Are facility-count bootstrap intervals available? | `bootstrap_allocation()` after an eligible fit and observation declaration | Conditional pointwise intervals when the supported procedure's gates pass |

An FCA index is not a choice probability. A fitted model is not automatically
identified or empirically validated. A regional interval is not a cellwise map
interval. These distinctions remain even when both workflows use the same
travel data.

## One Cornwall system, two calculations

Both calculations below use the same bundled open data for mainland Cornwall:
336 small areas (LSOAs) and 54 GP practices. The Isles of Scilly have no road
link to the mainland and are dropped. Demand is the residents of each area
registered with any GP practice in England (NHS England, July 2026), supply is
GP full-time equivalents (FTE) excluding GPs in training, and travel is
motorised minutes from each area's population-weighted centroid to each
practice.

```{r shared-inputs}
areas <- sf::st_drop_geometry(cornwall_lsoa)
gp <- sf::st_drop_geometry(cornwall_gp)
areas <- areas[!areas$scilly, ]
gp <- gp[!gp$scilly, ]

D <- setNames(areas$registered, areas$lsoa)
S <- setNames(gp$gp_fte_extg, gp$practice)
T <- cornwall_travel[areas$lsoa, gp$practice]
c(areas = length(D), practices = length(S), missing_travel = sum(is.na(T)))
```

### An FCA index

The public FCA functions take a demand raster and one travel layer per
facility. To give the FCA exactly the same demand and travel as the allocation
model, place the 336 areas in a one-row raster. The raster is only a container
without geographic meaning; values are mapped back to the areas afterwards.
The Gaussian scale of 10 minutes is a choice for this guide, not an estimate.

```{r fca}
template <- terra::rast(nrows = 1, ncols = length(D), xmin = 0,
  xmax = length(D), ymin = 0, ymax = 1, crs = "EPSG:27700")
demand_raster <- terra::setValues(template, unname(D))
travel_raster <- terra::rast(template, nlyrs = ncol(T))
terra::values(travel_raster) <- T
names(travel_raster) <- colnames(T)

fca <- spax_e2sfca(demand_raster, gp, travel_raster,
  decay_params = list(method = "gaussian", sigma = 10),
  id_col = "practice", supply_cols = c("gp_fte_extg", "gp_fte"))
fca_index <- 1000 * terra::values(fca$accessibility, dataframe = TRUE)
summary(fca_index)
```

Each supply column gives its own index, in GP FTE per 1,000 distance-weighted
registered residents: `gp_fte_extg` excludes GPs in training and `gp_fte`
includes them. The two are separate indicators computed side by side; the FCA
does not combine them.

### A static CLM fitted to registrations

The static CLM gives practice j an attraction S_j times its Gaussian decay
weight, and divides by the sum of attractions plus an outside weight v0. Each
area therefore has a probability for every practice plus an outside
probability, and these sum to 1. Here the outside option stands for
registration with a practice outside mainland Cornwall (for example in Devon
or on the Isles of Scilly); it is not unmet need. The model uses one supply
vector.

Fitting needs a declared target. Here it is the observed small area × practice
registrations, a stock of who is registered where rather than a count of
visits, fitted with a Poisson loss from three explicit starts.

```{r clm}
observed <- matrix(0, nrow(T), ncol(T), dimnames = dimnames(T))
keep <- cornwall_flows$lsoa %in% rownames(T) &
  cornwall_flows$practice %in% colnames(T)
observed[cbind(cornwall_flows$lsoa[keep], cornwall_flows$practice[keep])] <-
  cornwall_flows$patients[keep]

inputs <- prepare_allocation(D, S, T, metadata = list(
  demand_units = "registered residents", demand_period = "July 2026",
  supply_units = "GP FTE excluding GPs in training", supply_period = "June 2026",
  travel_units = "minutes"))
model <- clm_allocation(inputs, family = "gaussian", fit_v0 = TRUE)
starts <- rbind(near = c(sigma = 3, v0 = 0.05), middle = c(sigma = 6, v0 = 0.01),
  far = c(sigma = 12, v0 = 0.002))
fit <- fit_allocation(model, observed, starts,
  lower = c(sigma = 0.5, v0 = 1e-6), upper = c(sigma = 60, v0 = 10),
  output = "flow", loss = "poisson", gradient = TRUE,
  control = list(maxit = 300, factr = 10, pgtol = 1e-8))
stopifnot(identical(fit$status, "selected"))
coef(fit)
```

```{r clm-values, include = FALSE}
sigma_hat <- round(coef(fit)[["sigma"]], 1)
```

The fitted Gaussian scale is about `r sigma_hat` minutes, much shorter than
the 10 minutes chosen for the FCA: registration is very local. Inspect
`summary(fit)` for all starts, failures and boundaries; agreement among starts
does not establish identification or a global optimum.

## What one area sees

Take the area with the largest total FCA weight, one with many practices
within a short drive. The table lists its four nearest practices.

```{r one-area}
prediction <- predict_allocation(fit, T, demand = D,
  outputs = c("allocation", "outside_share"))
P <- prediction$outputs$allocation
W <- exp(-T^2 / (2 * 10^2))  # the FCA's Gaussian weights
i <- which.max(rowSums(W))
nearest <- order(T[i, ])[1:4]
data.frame(practice = gp$name[nearest], minutes = T[i, nearest],
  fca_weight = round(W[i, nearest], 2), clm_probability = round(P[i, nearest], 3),
  observed_share = round(observed[i, nearest] / D[i], 3), row.names = NULL)
round(c(fca_weights = sum(W[i, ]), clm_inside = sum(P[i, ]),
  clm_outside = prediction$outputs$outside_share[[i]]), 4)
```

The FCA weights are separate distance discounts, one per practice. They do not
compete with each other and they sum to far more than 1 here. The CLM
probabilities do compete: a nearby practice with more GP FTE draws residents
away from the others, and the probabilities over all practices plus the
outside option sum to 1. Lander Medical Practice, 7 minutes away with about
10 GP FTE, gets a higher probability than Chacewater Health Centre, 6 minutes
away with under 4. Because they are probabilities, they can be set beside the
observed shares of registered residents, which here differ markedly: the
model has no term for anything other than travel time and GP FTE.

## Side by side

The FCA returns one index per area for each supply column. The CLM returns a
distribution over practices for each area, from which other quantities follow:
expected flows (demand times probability), practice loads (their column sums)
and, for example, the mean travel time to the practice an area's residents are
modelled to register with.

```{r maps, fig.show = "hold", out.width = "49%", fig.width = 4.5, fig.height = 4.5}
areas$fca <- fca_index$gp_fte_extg
areas$clm_minutes <- rowSums(P * T) / rowSums(P)
mapped <- merge(cornwall_lsoa[, "lsoa"], areas)

ggplot(mapped) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = fca, colour = fca), linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "GP FTE\nper 1,000", aesthetics = c("fill", "colour")) +
  labs(title = "E2SFCA index (sigma = 10 min)") +
  theme_void()
ggplot(mapped) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = clm_minutes, colour = clm_minutes), linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Minutes", option = "magma", direction = -1,
    aesthetics = c("fill", "colour")) +
  labs(title = "CLM: mean minutes to modelled practice") +
  theme_void()
```

The FCA map shows supply relative to distance-weighted demand. The CLM map
shows how far residents are modelled to travel to their practice, longest in
rural areas in the north-east and at the western tip. The fitted flows can be
checked against the registrations; the FCA index has
no corresponding observed quantity in these data.

```{r check}
observed_minutes <- rowSums(observed * T) / rowSums(observed)
c(mean_minutes = cor(areas$clm_minutes, observed_minutes),
  practice_totals = cor(colSums(fitted(fit)), colSums(observed)))
outside <- c(observed = 1 - sum(observed) / sum(D),
  modelled = 1 - sum(fitted(fit)) / sum(D))
round(100 * outside, 2)
```

```{r check-values, include = FALSE}
r_min <- round(cor(areas$clm_minutes, observed_minutes), 2)
r_tot <- round(cor(colSums(fitted(fit)), colSums(observed)), 2)
```

Modelled and observed mean travel times correlate at `r r_min` across areas,
and modelled and observed practice totals at `r r_tot`. One constant outside
weight understates registration outside mainland Cornwall (the last line, in
per cent of registered residents), which is concentrated in a few areas near
the Devon border.

| | E2SFCA index | Static CLM |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Per area | One supply-per-demand score per supply column | A probability for each practice plus the outside option |
| Supply | Each column is a separate indicator | One supply vector, which sets attraction |
| Distance decay | Chosen by the analyst (10 minutes here) | Fitted to the declared target (about `r sigma_hat` minutes here) |
| Outside option | None | Explicit weight v0, fitted here |
| Check against registrations | No observed counterpart | Fitted flows, practice totals and outside share |

The table and maps place distinct measures beside one another; they are not
an equivalence check or a ranking of model quality. Neither output measures
delivered care, and supply in the CLM affects attraction; it is not a hard
capacity limit.

## The allocation verbs

The six experimental verbs are **prepare, declare, fit, evaluate, predict and
bootstrap**. They are separate steps so that a chosen fixed model can be
evaluated without fitting, while an eligible fit can be inspected without
refitting. An outside option does not automatically represent unmet need, and
Poisson fitting does not impose exact total matching.

This guide is not an uncertainty demonstration. The facility-case bootstrap
needs a fit to whole facility counts, so the flow fit above is outside its
scope. Continue to the [full allocation workflow](allocation-workflow.html)
for the generated 80-origin, 40-facility example with all 399 bootstrap
attempts, at least 380 finite successful values per reported quantity, paired
supply scenarios and fresh-process saved-result inspection. Observation
declarations and original-fit eligibility remain required; a bootstrap is not
available for every fit.

## Carry these checks across workflows

Use stable facility IDs, declare counts versus densities and reference periods,
and check travel geometry and units before computing. Keep zero demand, unknown
demand and absent travel edges distinct. Legacy FCA reductions and experimental
allocation preparation have different missing-data policies; sharing a file
does not prove that their included support is the same.

For details, read [data preparation](spax-102-data-prep.html),
[the FCA calculation](spax-103-dissection.html),
[resolution and cost](spax-104-raster-tradeoff.html), and
[saved-result inspection](function-naming.html).
